title: Developers Reporting Double-Digit Weekly Time Savings From AI Fell From 68% to 26%
summary:
Atlassian’s State of Developer Experience 2026 finds the share of developers saving ten or more hours a week with AI dropped from 68% to 26% year over year, while only 28% report noticeably less friction than before AI. Engineering leaders report spending more time managing and correcting AI output than developers do.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

Facilitating the Spread of Knowledge and Innovation in Professional Software Development Unlock the full InfoQ experience by logging in! Stay updated with your favorite authors and topics, engage with content, and download exclusive resources. Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. She shares how engineering teams can replace Python bottlenecks with Rust via PyO3, demonstrating how to achieve dramatic function-level speedups, seamless integration testing, and meaningful infrastructure cost savings without microservice overhead. Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. Chains are simple but fragile, graphs add branching, retries, and validation, and code harnesses verify outputs through execution. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs. Manju Rajashekhar explains how the actor model solves the complex runtime challenges of production AI agents. By treating agents as distributed systems, he discusses state ownership, message passing, write-through state, and supervision boundaries to manage failures, continuations, and mutable execution graphs, moving agentic workflows beyond fragile demos to resilient architecture. Nathen Harvey shares insights from DORA research on AI adoption in software delivery. He explains why AI acts as an amplifier, how the DORA AI Capabilities Model drives outcomes, and why engineering leaders must evolve beyond bottlenecks like code reviews to achieve sustainable productivity, reduce delivery instability, and empower developers without burning out their teams. Andrew Martin discusses why AI security is fundamentally tied to Kubernetes security. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments. title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks
summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
summary: Activation steering offers training-free and dynamic control of target behaviors in large language models, but existing methods can impair general capabilities and require domain-specific intervention designs. We introduce Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering (CANS), a unified framework that balances target-behavior control with capability preservation. To make target-behavior improvement and general-capability preservation tractable, we introduce two proxies: log-probabilities of target tokens in model generated responses, and output-distribution KL divergence on general-purpose inputs. Combining the local approximation of the two proxies yields a closed-form solution, enabling lightweight steering without iterative model training or additional inference-time computation. The resulting neuron-wise scaling coefficients achieve effective steering while limiting general-capability loss. A shared data-construction and intervention procedure supports adaptation across domains using sampled responses with target-behavior filtering and target-span annotations. Across safety, toxicity, and hallucination control on Qwen and Llama models, CANS achieves comparable or better steering while better preserving MMLU, BBH, and IFEval performance than SFT, CAA, and neuron-level baselines. On Qwen3-4B, CANS reduces HarmBench attack success from $15.50\%$ to $1.75\%$ with a $1.11$-point decrease in average capability. These results support CANS as a practical approach to behavioral control across domains.

title: AT-AT: Automatic Tool Optimization from Agent Traces
summary: Efforts to improve LLM-based agents typically focus on modifying the agent itself, yet success also depends on the environment in which an agent acts. Tools mediate this interaction: a tool's description shapes how an agent calls it, and its implementation determines the results and errors the agent receives afterwards. Many tools, such as APIs and MCP servers, are shared by many agents and maintained by providers who cannot change those agents. We introduce AT-AT (Automatic Tool Optimization from Agent Traces), an agentic tool optimizer that improves a shared toolset offline from historical agent executions while holding the agents fixed. A lightweight coding agent reads agent trajectories and their evaluation results, and selectively edits tool descriptions and, when permitted, implementations. On $τ^2$-bench-verified, AT-AT achieves the highest task completion rates in the Airline and Telecom domains at lower cost than strong prompt- and tool-optimizer baselines, and its Telecom gain is statistically significant under paired permutation tests. Optimizing the tools within a coding agent harness also improves held-out performance on TerminalBench-2 and TBLite. When applied to three production MCP servers at a large enterprise, AT-AT lowered cost or tool error rates on every server and increased held-out task passes on one. By turning accumulated execution traces into updates to shared tool environments, AT-AT provides a path toward continual improvement of agent systems through environment-side learning.

title: Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at Scale: vLLM Matches DeepInfer and Scales to GB300 NVL72
summary: With P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP on a GB300 NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 954K tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 196 tokens/s per user, 7.9x our aggregated single-node result.
story_key: model:deepseek|ver:4.1|variant:flash|title:serving deepseek v4 1 flash at scale vllm matches deepinfer and scales to gb300
content_excerpt: TL;DR: On one NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 rack, vLLM with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 954K tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 196 tokens/s per user, 7.9× our single-node result from the first post and $38.96 per GPU-hour at DeepSeek's off-peak prices. A specialized decode path reaches 826 tokens/s for a single user. Against DeepInfer, DeepSeek's own engine, vLLM's decode throughput is within 6% across batch sizes 8–256, and its prefill tracks DeepInfer's published curve. The efficiency comes from deliberate engineering on components that vLLM already has, built on the kernels DeepSeek open-sourced. This post walks through our performance study, breaks down each optimization, and shares the lessons we learned: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72: vLLM with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP (gold) achieves a further 7.9× throughput increase over our aggregated single-node result from the first post . Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( source ). DeepInfer is DeepSeek's own inference engine for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, released this week as an offline engine with published prefill and decode curves. It is the most relevant reference for this model, so before going into our optimizations we show where vLLM stands against it. Decode. Under DeepSeek's decode configuration (131K context, nextn=3), vLLM on GB200 achieves throughput within 6% of DeepInfer's published results across batch sizes 8 to 256 (Figure 2). Figure 2: Decode output throughput per GPU vs. batch size at 131K context, nextn=3. vLLM on GB200 vs. DeepInfer's published results, read from the charts in its README ( source ). Prefill. DeepInfer's published prefill curve uses EP4DP4 with 32 redundant experts and a 140-token bounded replay, on hardware the chart does not state, and we read its values off the chart. Our run uses DEP2 on GB300 with no redundant experts, a 128-token replay and our own prompts. Because the setups differ, we do not read the gap between the two curves as an engine-to-engine speedup. What Figure 3 shows is that vLLM's DEP2 prefill tracks DeepSeek's own engine across the range they published. Figure 3: Prefill throughput vs. new tokens. vLLM DEP2 on GB300 vs. DeepInfer's published curve (EP4DP4, 32 redundant experts, 140-token replay, hardware not stated), read from the chart in its README ( source ). title: MarkovSim: an LLM Agent Harness with Bounded Context for Long-Horizon Computational Simulation
summary: Recent studies have applied large language model (LLM) agent systems to computational simulation workflows. Such workflows are long-horizon, so the information generated can exceed what an LLM can reason over at once, its context window. Context management is therefore essential, yet existing systems have either neglected it or treated it as a supporting mechanism rather than a subject of study. This paper presents MarkovSim, an LLM agent harness for long-horizon computational simulation, whose core is a context management scheme built into the workflow. The workflow record is written to a memory system with a predefined schema, and at workflow-defined boundaries, namely the state transitions of a finite-state machine a compact representation of the solution progress is constructed from it as the agent's context. Instantiated on finite element analysis and evaluated on six benchmark problems, MarkovSim passed 16 of 18 runs and corrected its own faults in both the solver operations and the model physics. The engineer was consulted only where engineering judgement was needed. The context remained bounded throughout every run, regardless of its length.

title: Logic Hijacking of RAG: Single-Document Poisoning via Local Optimization
summary: Single-document corpus poisoning under black-box access poses a severe threat to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). However, existing attacks predominantly rely on explicit factual refutations or imperative instruction overrides. Modern aligned LLMs often arbitrate such conflicts conservatively, rejecting overt contradictions in favor of parametric memory or clean retrieved context while triggering input guardrails. We propose MONOLOGUE, a single-document poisoning framework based on Logic Hijacking without explicit refutation. Rather than disputing the ground truth, our method concedes it as an authoritative historical baseline before introducing the update, weaving a grounded record-correction narrative (e.g., dated institutional reattributions) that presents the counterfactual target as the most recent update. To prevent suspicious live writes, payloads are refined entirely offline via local multi-dimensional gated optimization, coupling automated text quality audits with surrogate behavioral verification. Evaluations across three benchmarks, three retrieval backends, and four open-weight generator regimes show that our method achieves the strongest overall attack efficacy among the evaluated single-document poisoning attacks.

title: claude-code v2.1.305
summary:
What's changed

  • Added sandbox.allowNestedUserNamespaces so sandboxed commands on Linux can create user namespaces (Chromium, rootless podman); this lets them get around the sandbox's file protections
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_USAGE_LIMIT_RECHECK_MS so unattended retry mode (CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG) notices a usage limit that was lifted before its reset
  • Fixed every request failing on Vertex, Bedrock and other providers when the endpoint or a gateway rejects tool search, and behind gateways with ToolSearch disallowed or left out of --tools (a 2.1.304 regression): Claude Code now retries without it
  • Fixed /effort and /autocompact settings not applying when the model name differed from a modelOverrides value by letter case or a [1m] tag
  • Fixed new worktrees in a bare repository sometimes starting from local HEAD instead of the default branch, and unchanged subagent worktrees sometimes not being cleaned up
  • Fixed Bash commands on a full disk failing with a raw ENOSPC file path: the error now says the disk is full and that nothing ran
  • Fixed an MCP server passed by a cloud session or by the SDK's setMcpServers being replaced later in the session by a same-named server from your own settings
  • Fixed Claude naming the wrong model for a subagent's work after the subagent switched to a fallback model
  • Fixed cloud sessions and teammates not telling Claude when a compaction had to leave the oldest messages out of its summary to fit
  • Fixed more cases of scheduled Cowork cloud sessions waiting five minutes for each subagent whose WebFetch needed a URL approval that nobody was there to give
  • Fixed Workflow resume re-running already-completed pipeline() and parallel() agents instead of serving them from the run's journal
  • Fixed Remote Control leaving empty "(session)" entries in /resume after switching conversations with /resume
  • Fixed /usage rows being cut off in narrow terminals
  • Fixed startup warnings printing as raw text above the logo: they now go to the debug log, and permission rules that restrict nothing show as warning rows under the banner
  • Fixed screen reader mode: search boxes now say "Search:" instead of a symbol VoiceOver read as "telephone recorder", and highlighted prompt text, such as Ctrl+R search matches and "ultrathink", no longer has spaces inside words
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a start script that shares only its stdout with the runner or orchestrator failing with Resource temporarily unavailable when TERM is set (a 2.1.300 regression)
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed repository access failing since 2.1.296 when a git credential helper or askpass program reads its settings through GIT_CONFIG
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed the orchestrator reporting a spawn-runner hook as timed out when a runner it started in the background kept its output open
  • Improved /usage: each warning is now a one-line fix that names its source, and f applies the fixes; the same fixes appear in VS Code and /doctor
  • Improved MCP consent dialogs so an Enter meant for the prompt is less likely to be taken as Accept
  • Improved a mod's Image to draw its picture in iTerm2 3.5 and later with fullscreen rendering, where it showed only its alt text
  • Remote Control: Improved the spawn-mode messages: pressing w now says the new mode is saved for the folder, and a later claude remote-control start that uses the saved mode says where it came from
  • Changed allowedMcpServers to stop filtering managed-mcp.json stdio servers that use ${VAR} only in env: one your allowlist left out now loads on upgrade; use deniedMcpServers to keep it off
  • Changed plugins that Claude Desktop mounts by path to no longer keep their allowed-tools when your organization's managed settings set allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly
  • Changed the /artifacts delete confirmation to take 1 or Enter to keep, 2 to delete, and Esc to cancel; y and n no longer answer it
  • Changed a mod's docked pane to stay within 45% of the terminal's width, including a width kept from a wider terminal
  • [VSCode] Added a "Running start-up hooks" spinner status, with a screen reader announcement, while SessionStart or Setup hooks run
  • [VSCode] Fixed the spinner cutting off "Compacting..." when your spinnerVerbs setting replaces the built-in verbs with short ones
  • [VSCode] Changed the message shown when a session does not start in time and no hook is running: it now leads with the output logs and lists causes instead of pointing to sign-in and network first
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the Cloud environments admin page wrongly refusing to save an existing environment with an "installs packages" error
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved deleting a self-hosted environment so the dialog and error messages say what blocks the delete and what it will affect
  • [Claude Tag] Added public Slack channels Claude hasn't joined to the Claude Tag admin Add place search, so admins can set one up from there
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag access bundles so a repository that moved to another GitHub account can be added again
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a routine set up in a Slack DM thread no longer posting after another routine in that thread restarted the conversation; both now keep posting there
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed routines set up in a Slack thread reporting success without posting after the conversation ended; those runs are now skipped and the creator is told
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag admin pages in large organizations so plugin, skill and bundle edits work while the channel list is still loading
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review sometimes not reviewing the newest commit when several pushes landed on a pull request during a review
  • [Code Review] Changed Code Review re-reviews so they no longer open with LGTM while earlier blocking findings are still open
